hostParish.name: Most Sacred Heart of Jesus Parish

history.title: History
history.body:
The year 2009 marked the golden jubilee of the Roman Catholic Parish of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus in San Isidro, a Northern Samar municipality which has been in existence since the year 1954.

San Isidro - the seat of the parish erected fifty years ago - was once called Calagundian. The name Calagundian was derived from Lagundi, a large native shrub that once thrived on the coast of the place.

Samarnons and many other Filipinos traditionally. used Lagundi or Vitex Negundo as cure for asthma and fever caused by cold and flu, rheumatism, dyspepsia, boils, leprosy, diarrhea and cholera. Farmers of old also used to burn Lagundi leaves when warding off insects and pests.

The place was renamed San Isido after its holy advocate, San Isidro Labrador or Saint Isidore the Farmer, whose feast falls on the 15 day of May. The godly cultivator from Madrid, Spain was born in 1070 and died in 1130. He was canonized by Pope Urban VIll in 1632 and is now venerated universally as patron of rural life.

The golden anniversary of the Parish occurred one thousand and nine hundred seventy six years after the carpenter Jesus of Nazareth founded the one, holy, apostolic and catholic Church in the year 33 A. D. and entrusted it to the fisherman Simon Peter from Bethsaida in Galilee.

The celebration also occurred four hundred and thirteen years after the evangelization of the historic island of Samar. Christianity was introduced to the natives of Ibabao or Samar by Spanish missionaries Fr Francisco de Otazo, Fr. Bartolome Martes and Bro.Domingo Alonso on October 15, 1596.

Ibabao was the ancient name for Samar. Ibabao was dubbed as "the land above" as another island lies "below" it, that of Irate which is now called Leyte. The present name of the third largest and easternmost island of the Philippines is said to have been derived from the word "samad" which means wound in the language of its people. The name apparently refers to the geographic nature of the island - a land mass 1.342 million hectares or 5,750 square miles in its entirety - which is dissected by mountains, valleys and rivers. Bisaya-Samarnon is one of the three major languages of the Visayas group of islands, the other two being Bisaya-Hiligaynon of Western Visayas and Bisaya-Sugbuanon of Central Visavas Spanish colonizers who noticed the tattooed people of the Visayas then called the islands Las Islas de Pintados.

Around a century and a halt ago, the site of what was become Calagundian in later years was within the jurisdiction of the old parroquia or parish of Calbayog before it developed into a formal community.

The old Roman Catholic missions of Catubig (San Jose Patriarca), Palapag (Asuncion de Nuestra Señora), Capul (San Ignacio de Loyola), Catarman (Anunciacion de Nuestra Señora), Calbayog (Natividad de Nuestra Señora) as well as the entire island of Samar once formed part of the old Diocesis de Cebu or Diocese of Cebu which was established by Pope Clement VIII on August 14, 1595 under the tutelage of the Santisimo Nobre de Jesus or the Most Holy Name of Jesus Bishop Pedro de Agurto was the first prelate of Cebu.

The Diocese of Cebu then covered not only the islands of Cebu and Samar but Bohol, Leyte, Negros, Panay, Mindanao and the Marianas in the Pacific. It was originally under the jurisdiction of the old Diocese of Manila which was erected by Pope Gregory XIII on February. 6, 1578 under the advocacy of La Purisima Inmaculada Concepcion de Nuestra Señora or Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception. Bishop Domingo de Salazar was the first prelate of Manila. He belonged to the Orden de Santo Domingo or the Ordo Praedicatorum (OP), a congregation founded by Saint Dominic de Guzman in France in the year 1206.

Cebu is considered as the birthplace of Christianity in the Philippines. It was in Cebu where Fernão de Magalhães or Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese serving the Spanish royalty, erected a wooden cross in 1521. The image of the Santo Niño de Cebu was given to Rajah Humabon’s wife Ratu Humanay by Antonio Pigafetta, the Italian chronicler of Magellan’s expedition, on the day Fr. Pedro Valderrama baptized and eight hundred other Sugbuanon.

The oldest Samar missions were founded by missionaries of the Campania de Jesus or the Societas Jesu (SJ) which Saint Ignatius of Loyola established in France in the year 1634. Capul, known as Abac in ancient times, was one of the first missions established bu the Jesuits in northern Samar after the missionaries reached Catubig and Palapag. The Jesuits decided to establish their residencia or central residence in Palapag and made the pueblo the cabecera or center of their missions. Palapag's ecclesiastical domain originally covered the visitas of Catubig, Laoang, Pambujan, Catarman and Bobon. The visitas of Calbayog, Matnog, Sta. Magdalena and Bulusan were initially under the ecclesiastical sphere of Capul.

A pueblo during the Spanish colonial rule referred to a municipality. The poblacion was the core of a pueblo wherein a gobernadorcillo wielded political power from the micipio and wherein a cura parroco exercised ecclesiastical authority from the iglesia, both of which were usually located around a plaza mayor that usually served as apoint of origin for calles or streets lined with casas or houses belonging to the principalia or the local elite.

A visita at the time meant a village with a chapel that received periodic visits from the cura parroco or priest of the pueblo having ecclesiastical jurisdiction over the community. The cura parroco usually devoted his visits to the celebration of Mass or the propagation of Christian doctrines and precepts among the people.

Palapag and Capul both figured in the chronicles of the Manila-Acapulco galleon trade which began in 1565 and ended in 1815. A royal naval station was established in Palapag while Capul was designated as a was station for the galleons. Agustin Sumuroy and the babaonons of Palapag carved a niche for their pueblo in Philippine history when they rejected the conscription order of Governor-General Diego Fajardo and commenced the Palapag Revolt on June 1, 1649. Sumuroy was a commandant of the garrison and sentinel of the galleons in Palapag. He descended from a line of babaonon seafarers who sailed the famous Tagbaloran in ancient times. Tagbaloran was the ancient name for the Embocadero or Estrecho de San Bernardino, the famous strait that separates the islands of Luzon and Samar.

Sumuroy and many other natives who refused to be sent to the shipyard in Cavite attacked the cura parroco Fr. Miguel Ponce Barberan and scked the iglesia and convento of Palapg. The Sumuroy-led revolt spread to Camarines, Albay, Sorsogon, Masbate, Leyte, Cebu, Zamboanga, Misamis, Agusan and Surigao and was described as the most widespread revolt prior to the Philippine Revolution against Spain.

Barely a century after the revolt in Palapag, the twin islands of Smar and Leyte that were both under the political jurisdiction of Cebu since 1565 were created into a separate province in 1747 with the pueblo of Catbalogan as its capital. Catbalogan became the cabecera of the Jesuit missions in western Samar after the Moro raids of 1612-1616 devastated the very first Jesuit mission in Tinagon which was then located in what should become pueblo Tarangnan.

priestMessage.title: Parish Priest's Message
priestMessage.subtitle: Fr. Prospero Elmo Cabili
priestMessage.body:
My dear young people,

As you gather for the Diocesan Youth Day 2026, I see in you the living hope of the Church. You are not just the future — you are the present, vibrant face of Christ in our Diocese.

May this DYD be more than just an event, but a true encounter — an encounter with Christ, with one another, and with your deeper calling to serve. Carry the light you will receive here back to your parishes, to your families, and to your communities.

I am proud of our Working Committee and all our delegates who have offered their time, talent, and heart for this mission. Your service is already a prayer.

Walk together, pray together, and grow together as pilgrims of hope.

God bless you always!
priestMessage.signatoryAffiliation: Most Sacred Heart of Jesus Parish

associatePastorMessage.title: Associate Pastor's Message
associatePastorMessage.subtitle: Fr. Leo Almasco
associatePastorMessage.body:
My dear young pilgrims,

What a joy to see you journey together as one family in faith! Diocesan Youth Day is a beautiful reminder that you are never alone — you walk with Christ and with hundreds of young hearts who share the same love for Him.

My prayer is that in these days, you may truly listen. Listen to God who speaks in silence, in songs, in sharing, and in friendships. May you return home not just with memories and photos, but with a renewed heart ready to serve.

To our dear Working Committee, thank you for your generous yes. To all delegates, welcome! Enjoy, pray, and let your light shine.

May our Blessed Mother guide your steps.

In Christ,
associatePastorMessage.signatoryAffiliation: Most Sacred Heart of Jesus Parish

coordinatorMessage.title: Parish Youth Coordinator's Message
coordinatorMessage.subtitle: Jessa Mae Arcipe
coordinatorMessage.body:
"Take courage, I have overcome the world." - John 16:33

Maupay nga adlaw, mga Kalakbay!

As the Parish Youth Coordinator of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus Parish, your host parish, I joyfully welcome you to Diocesan Youth Day 2026!

Our theme this year reminds us that even when life feels heavy — with school, family, and many worries — Jesus tells us, "Take courage." He has already won for us.

As we celebrate 67 Years of Most Sacred Heart of Jesus Parish and 6 Years of Kabataan ni San Isidro PYM, this DYD becomes even more meaningful for us.

On behalf of all Kabataan ni San Isidro (KNSI), we are so excited and we are truly looking forward to seeing you all! We are preparing with so much love to make you feel at home.

This DYD is for you. This Parish is your Parish. This celebration is your celebration.

Let's find courage together in the Heart of Jesus.

Always remember, para sa ATIN ang DYD nato!

From our Sacred Heart to yours, welcome to DYD 2026!

With grateful heart,
coordinatorMessage.signatoryAffiliation: Most Sacred Heart of Jesus Parish - Host Parish

leaderMessage.title: Parish Youth Leader's Message
leaderMessage.subtitle: John Andrew Registos
leaderMessage.body:
To all the young people of the Diocese of Catarman,

As the Parish Youth Leader of the host parish, it is with great joy and excitement that we welcome all of you to Diocesan Youth Day 2026 here in San Isidro!

This gathering is more than just an event, it is an opportunity for us to come together as one community, strengthen our faith, build friendships, and encounter Christ in one another.

To every young person joining us, we hope you come with an open heart, ready to take courage, grow in faith, and walk together as pilgrims of hope.

From all of us here in the host parish, welcome home, mga Kalakbay! We are excited to journey with you!

This is DYD 2026! Let us take courage, for our Lord Jesus Christ has already overcome the world!

From our Sacred Heart to yours, welcome to DYD 2026!

With grateful heart,
leaderMessage.signatoryAffiliation: Most Sacred Heart of Jesus Parish - Host Parish

history.title: History
history.headline: HISTORY OF THE DIOCESAN YOUTH DAY (DYD)

sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
paragraphs: The Diocesan Youth Day (DYD) is one the highest and most significant gatherings of young people in the Diocese of Catarman. Inspired by the World Youth Day founded by St. John Paul II, the DYD is a pilgrimage of faith where the youth of Northern Samar journey as one Church — diverse yet united in Christ.

entries.title: 1st DYD: Mondragon (Dec. 13-15, 2002) — Hosted by St. Anthony of Padua Parish.
bullets: The pioneering moment that laid the foundation of the youth ministry in the diocese.

entries.title: 2nd DYD: Rosario (Dec. 5-7, 2003) — Hosted by Our Lady of the Most Holy Rosary Parish.
bullets: Strengthened the structure of the Diocesan Commission on Youth.

entries.title: 3rd DYD: Las Navas (Dec. 9-11, 2005) — Hosted by Our Lady of Nativity Parish.
bullets: Highlighted the missionary spirit of the youth in the hinterlands.

groups.title: The Great Revival in the Year of the Youth 2018

entries.title: 4th DYD: Catarman (Nov. 30 - Dec. 1, 2018) — Hosted by Our Lady of Annunciation, Cathedral
bullets: After 13 years of silence, the flame was rekindled at the most providential time. The year 2018 was declared as the YEAR OF THE YOUTH by the CBCP with the theme "Filipino Youth: Beloved, Gifted, Empowered." Dubbed as the "Revival DYD," it was held at the Cathedral Parish of Our Lady of Annunciation, Catarman — a powerful affirmation that the youth are truly beloved, gifted, and empowered.

groups.title: The New Era: The Journey of Hope and Courage

entries.title: 5th DYD: Pambujan (October 2025) — Hosted by St. John the Baptist Parish, Pambujan.
bullets: With the Jubilee theme, "Christ: Our Anchor of Hope," the 5th DYD marked the beginning of a new commitment to celebrate DYD annually. In a world full of uncertainty, the youth were reminded that our hope is firm because it is anchored in Christ.

entries.title: 6th DYD: San Isidro (October 17-18, 2026)
bullets: Now, the pilgrimage continues to the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus Parish, San Isidro. For the first time, San Isidro is honored to host the DYD with the theme "Take Courage: I Have Overcome the World" (John 16:33). From being anchored in hope, we are now called to be courageous. This historic celebration will also be marked by the Solemn Enthronement of the image of St. Pedro Calungsod from Cebu.

sections.heading: III. CONCLUSION
paragraphs: From St. Anthony of Padua Parish, Mondragon in 2002 to Most Sacred Heart of Jesus Parish, San Isidro in 2026, the 24-year journey of the DYD tells one story: God never abandons His young Church.
We were Beloved, Gifted, and Empowered in 2018, we found our Anchor of Hope in Christ in 2025, and now in 2026, Jesus Himself tells us: "Take Courage! I Have Overcome the World."

speakers.name: Most Rev. Bishop Juan Dela Cruz, D.D.
speakers.bio: Bishop Dela Cruz leads the diocese with a passion for youth evangelization and missionary discipleship. His opening message sets the tone for DYD 2026.

speakers.name: Rev. Fr. Michael Santos
speakers.bio: Fr. Michael serves as Diocesan Youth Director and has accompanied youth communities across the vicariates for over a decade.

speakers.name: Sr. Maria Clara Reyes, RVM
speakers.bio: Sr. Maria Clara is a religious educator who helps young people see holiness in ordinary life—school, family, and parish service.

speakers.name: Kent Veloso
speakers.bio: Kent is a parish youth leader from Lourdes Parish, Vicariate ABC. He shares practical ways youth can lead prayer, service, and community action.

speakers.name: Dr. Ana Villanueva
speakers.bio: Dr. Villanueva integrates faith with social action, mentoring student leaders in campus ministry and outreach programs.

speakers.name: Bro. James Mendoza, SDB
speakers.bio: Bro. James works with young people through education and recreation, inviting them to encounter Christ through joy and friendship.

guidelines.title: Dress Code
guidelines.body:
Please dress modestly in attire suitable for liturgical celebrations and outdoor activities.

We request that everyone wear the official DYD 2026 shirt in the color assigned to their vicariate:

• Red — Host Parish
• Blue — Allen Vicariate
• Green — Catarman Vicariate
• Yellow — Laoang Vicariate
• White — Palapag Vicariate

guidelines.title: House Rules
guidelines.body: Respect venue property. No smoking or alcohol. Follow ushers' instructions at all times.

guidelines.title: Safety Reminders
guidelines.body: Stay with your cluster. Know your assembly point. Report emergencies to the Medical & DRRM Team.
